Call highlights:
- Goal: integrate Redwood inference to support structured tool/function calling for FinApps' transaction enrichment flow (PDF parsing -> enrichment -> reranker + embeddings for similarity search).
- Integration areas discussed: SDK setup & auth, request routing (region/fallback/cost tiers), structured output vs tool calling, tool definitions, parallel tool orchestration, and embeddings/rerankers.
- Constraints: PII-safe processing (customer wants on-premise option later), bursty traffic with spiky peaks at EOD, and strict retry semantics for idempotent enrichment calls.

1) I attached a short SDK quickstart and a checklist (redwood-sdk-quickstart.pdf, finapps-integration-checklist.xlsx). Please share any sample endpoints/credentials we should expect.
2) Dev (cc'd) will follow up with recommended tool/function-calling patterns (tool definitions, error handling, parallel tools) and an implementation sketch.

- Typical payload sizes and expected concurrency per minute at peak?
- Any internal orchestration system (e.g., Airflow, Temporal) we should integrate with or observe?

Thanks Marissa — great summary. A few quick answers and questions before the deep-dive: 

- Auth: we prefer mTLS for service-to-service between our infra and partners, but could support short-lived API keys if needed for POC.
- Peak: our batch enrichment jobs hit ~1200 requests/minute during EOD spikes; single-request payloads are usually <200KB but can include base64-encoded PDF snippets.
- Orchestration: we use Temporal for async workflows and Kafka for eventing.

Technical questions we want covered in the deep-dive:

2) Do you support parallel tool invocation in a single call and how do you handle partial failures?
3) What retry/backoff semantics do you recommend for idempotent vs non-idempotent tools?
4) How are embeddings/reranker pipelines best integrated (sync vs async)?

Hi Emma — thanks for the quick answers. Below is a condensed tech note that I'll expand into a short doc (attached: tool-calling-patterns.md) for the deep-dive. High-level patterns for tool/function-calling integration with Redwood: 

1) Tool definitions (recommended schema)
- id: unique tool identifier (string)
- name: human-friendly
- inputs: typed schema (JSON Schema preferred)
- outputs: typed schema (JSON Schema)
- idempotency_key: boolean flag (whether calls can be retried safely)
- timeout_ms, max_retries, retry_policy (enum: none, exponential_backoff, linear)

Why typed schemas: structured inputs/outputs let the model produce validated JSON which simplifies orchestration and reduces brittle NLP parsing.

2) Tool choice: structured output vs explicit tool call
- Structured output (model returns JSON matching schema): good for simple transforms and extraction with low side-effects.
- Explicit tool calling (tool invoked by runtime): preferred for side-effecting operations (DB writes, external APIs) and when deterministic behavior & observability are required.

3) Parallel tools & orchestration
- Pattern A: fan-out within runtime — Redwood can issue several tool calls in parallel and aggregate results. Use when tools are independent and you want lower end-to-end latency.
- Pattern B: orchestrator-driven (Temporal/Kafka) — the model emits tasks which your orchestrator executes asynchronously; better for complex workflows, retries, and long-running operations.
- Aggregation: include correlation ids in tool responses and a final merge step to produce the enriched document.

4) Error handling + retries
- For idempotent tools: exponential backoff with jitter, limit retries to N (configurable per-tool), log each attempt with correlation_id.
- For non-idempotent tools: avoid automatic retries; instead, queue for manual or orchestrator-driven compensation flows.
- Partial failure strategy: return a result with tool-level statuses and let the caller decide to retry or fallback. Example response shape: {"tools": [{"id":"ocr","status":"ok","result":...}, {"id":"enrich","status":"error","error":"timeout"}]}

5) Auth & routing
- mTLS is fully supported on Dedicated/Private deployments; for Hosted we recommend short-lived tokens + origin allow-listing.
- Routing: policy-based (latency-first vs cost-first) — Redwood can route to regional endpoints or lower-cost quantized model variants as a fallback.

6) Embeddings & rerankers
- For similarity search at query-time: compute embeddings on ingestion and store vectors in your vector DB; call reranker as a final scoring step to improve recall/precision.
- Sync vs async: for low-latency enrichment keep reranking sync if dataset is small; for large corpora, use async batches and return a pending state with callback/webhook.

7) Observability & debugging
- Include per-request correlation_id, token-level cost, model-version metadata, and tool invocation logs.
- Provide a sample JSON schema for the final API response and error envelope.

I'll send a short markdown with examples ahead of the deep-dive. If your team prefers mTLS, we'll include a brief section on cert rotation and mutual auth.

Thanks,
